tagline.text: A banana-shaped island of snow-white sand and a floating bar on the sea

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: December–May (dry season); the sea is calmest March–May

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,200–4,000 per person (per day, excluding lodging)

children.text: A small island of about 16 hectares floating off Cadiz in northern Negros, ringed by cream-colored sand and shallow, emerald water. Famous for Tawhai, a large floating bar anchored offshore, it can be visited as a day trip from Bacolod.
Lakawon Island is a small island in the Visayan Sea, about
15–20 minutes

by boat from the Cadiz Viejo coast in Cadiz City, northern Negros Occidental. Fine white sand wraps around the elongated, curving, banana-shaped island, and the water stays waist-deep even far from shore, making it good for playing in the water with kids. The island's interior has coconut palms and grassy lawns, good for resting in the shade too.

The whole island is operated as Lakawon Island Resort, and you enter by paying the admission fee and round-trip boat fare together at the port. The beach has bamboo cottages, restaurants, a bar, and bungalows for overnight stays, and you can rent marine leisure gear like kayaks, paddleboards, and banana boats. Being well developed means it's less of a deserted-island escape, and on weekends and holidays it gets crowded with families from Bacolod and nearby cities.

What made Lakawon famous is Tawhai, a floating bar anchored offshore. Built on a large bamboo-and-timber raft with sunbeds and a bar, it lets you sip a drink, swim, and sunbathe surrounded by sea on every side. Introduced as Asia's largest floating bar when it opened, it has become one of Negros's signature photo spots.

It suits Bacolod and Silay travelers who want a white sand beach without traveling as far as Boracay or El Nido, families with kids, and anyone wanting a day of rest. If you're hoping for snorkeling spots or diving, Carbin Reef or Danjugan Island to the south are better choices.

Lie on a sunbed at the large floating bar offshore and enjoy the feeling of being in the middle of the sea. Operating days and hours are fixed, and there's often a separate fee, so check at the port first.
The beach on the island's south side slopes gently, so you can wade far out. At low tide, a sandbar emerges, creating a scene of water in layered shades of color.
In the calm of the morning, rent a kayak (about
per hour) or a paddleboard and tour around the island and the floating bar.

blocks.title: A beach walk around the island

children.text: Walking all the way around the island takes about
30–40 minutes
. The island's north end, with fewer resort facilities, is relatively quiet and good for photos.
Once the day-trippers have left, the island takes on an entirely different atmosphere. Staying overnight lets you enjoy the beach at dusk and an unlit night sky in peace.
Rent a beach cottage and enjoy grilled food and seafood with your group. You can order from the resort restaurant, and check the outside-food policy before your visit.

children.text: Group water sports like banana boats and round tube rides are popular for trips with friends or family. Rates vary by group size and duration.

The
December–May
dry season is best.
December–February
sees some windy, slightly choppier days from the northeast monsoon (Amihan), but little rain.
March–May

brings the calmest sea and clearest water, ideal for the floating bar and kayaking. On the other hand, the island gets very crowded during Holy Week and summer-vacation weekends, with longer waits for the boat.
June–November

is the wet season, with frequent afternoon showers and cloudy days, and boat service is suspended by coast guard order when a typhoon approaches. If visiting during the wet season, it's safer to go in early in the morning and leave before the afternoon rain. Every
January
, Cadiz City holds the Dinagsa Festival honoring the Santo Niño, and the town is lively during this period.

items.label: Island accommodation
items.note: Fan cottage to air-conditioned room, for 4–6 people

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary depending on local conditions.
Lodging on the island is limited to resort-run fan cottages, air-conditioned rooms, and family villas, at about

a night for 4–6 people. Room numbers are limited, so book weeks ahead for weekends and peak season. Most travelers stay in Bacolod or Silay and visit as a day trip, and Cadiz town also has small hotels and pensions, convenient for catching an early boat.

Island restaurants serve Filipino-style seafood, grilled dishes, fried rice, and simple pasta. Grilled shrimp, grilled squid, and fish sinigang (a tangy soup) are safe bets, and the floating bar sells beer, cocktails, and fruit shakes. Prices on the island run higher than on the mainland, so it's good to bring a bit of your own water and snacks. On the way back, buying local products like dried fish and coconut vinegar at the Cadiz market, or returning to Bacolod for a chicken inasal dinner, are both popular ways to end the trip.
Regular boats only depart once full, so arriving at the port around
keeps your wait short.
The floating bar sometimes operates mainly on weekends or limits how long you can stay at once. If visiting on a weekday, ask in advance whether it's open.
Beach cottages are first-come, first-served, so arriving earlier gets you a better shaded spot.
There's no ATM on the island, and some places don't accept cards, so bring plenty of cash.
This is mostly a sandy sea with almost no coral reef for snorkeling. To see coral and fish, combine your trip with Carbin Reef in Sagay.
The sandy beach has little shade, so UV exposure is very strong. Bring a rash guard, a hat, and reef-safe sunscreen.
The island gets crowded on weekends and holidays, so go on a weekday if you want a quiet beach.
A waterproof bag and a change of clothes will ease worries about getting wet when boarding and disembarking the boat.

If traveling as a group, chartering a van for the day in Bacolod to cover Lakawon, Carbin Reef, and the Sagay coast in one trip takes much less time than switching buses. Agree on the driver's meal allowance and waiting-time terms before you set out.
Admission fees, boat charges, and how the floating bar operates change often depending on the resort. Check the resort's latest notices before visiting, and book a day ahead if needed.
Boat service stops during typhoon warnings or strong winds. Don't force a departure on bad-weather days.
Swimming after drinking at the floating bar is dangerous. Wear a life jacket, and always keep children within a guardian's sight.
Sea urchins and jellyfish can be present even in shallow water, so wear aqua shoes.
If you miss the last return boat, you'll need to call an expensive special trip. Be sure to confirm the return time.
Tricycles soliciting passengers around the Cadiz bus stop and the port charge inconsistent fares. Before getting in, clearly agree whether it's chartered or shared, and one way or round trip.
Pack out your trash in the bag you brought it in, and don't take shells or coral from the beach.
